html:
In the 1990s the government of Saddam Hussein drained most of the Mesopotamian Marshes, a vast wetland where the Tigris and Euphrates meet in southern Iraq, home to the Marsh Arabs for thousands of years.

The marshes sheltered rebels after the 1991 uprisings. Canals and dykes diverted the rivers, and by 2000 about 90 percent of the marshes had dried into salt flats. Villages of reed houses were burned, and most of the Marsh Arabs, perhaps a quarter of a million people, were driven out. Birds and fish vanished.

After the Iraq War in 2003, local people broke the dykes and part of the marshes came back. In 2016 they became a World Heritage Site. Dams upstream and drought still threaten them. See also Iraq.
sum: In the 1990s the government of Saddam Hussein drained most of the Mesopotamian Marshes, a vast wetland where the Tigris and Euphrates meet in southern Iraq, home to the Marsh Arabs for thousands of years.
